lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Well, Alexander, you can hardly deny now that you're my son. You wouldn't be dead if you were Ammon's.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: I knew perfectly well, father, that I was the son of Philip son of Amyntas. I just accepted the oracle because I thought it would come in useful.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: Useful? You thought it was useful to make a public spectacle of letting yourself be conned by priests?

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: Not that. It was the barbarians — they were terrified of me. Nobody resisted any more, because they thought they were fighting a god. So I beat them more easily.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: And which of these opponents was actually worth beating? You spent your whole career fighting cowards with little bows and little shields and wickerwork. [pause] Greeks would have been work — Boeotians, Phocians, Athenians. The Arcadian heavy infantry. Thessalian cavalry. Elean javelin-men. The Mantinean peltasts. Thracians, Illyrians, even Paeonians — taking them down, that would be something. Medes and Persians and Chaldaeans? Men in gold jewellery and soft slippers? You do remember that ten thousand of them went up there with Clearchus before you — and beat the Persians without the Persians even waiting to come to grips. They ran before the arrows were in range.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: The Scythians though, father — and the Indian elephants. That wasn't trivial work. And I beat them without setting them against each other, without buying victories through treason. I never broke an oath, never gave my word and lied, never did anything underhanded for the sake of winning. And as for the Greeks — most of them came over without bloodshed. Though I imagine you've heard how I dealt with Thebes.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: I've heard all of it. Cleitus told me — the one you ran through with a spear at dinner, because he had the nerve to compliment me in comparison to you.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: And then you threw off the Macedonian cloak and put on — what do they call it — a kandys, and stuck an upright tiara on your head, and expected Macedonians, free men, to prostrate themselves in front of you. And the most ridiculous part of all: you started imitating the people you'd just defeated. I won't even get into the rest — locking educated men up with lions, the marriages you contracted, the way you carried on about Hephaestion. [pause] There was one thing I approved of when I heard it: that you kept your hands off Darius's wife, who was beautiful, and looked after his mother and daughters. That, at least, was kingly.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: What about my taste for danger, father? Don't you praise that? Being the first man over the wall at the Oxydracae, taking all those wounds?

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: No, Alexander, I don't praise it. Not because there's anything wrong with a king getting wounded sometimes or risking himself for the army — but because in your case it was the worst possible thing. You were claiming to be a god. So every time you got hit, every time they saw you carried out of battle on a stretcher, bleeding, groaning over your wound — that was a punchline. Right there it was proved that Ammon was a fraud, the oracle was a lie, and the priests were sycophants. [pause] Who wouldn't laugh, watching the son of Zeus pass out and beg the doctors to do something? And now that you're actually dead — you don't think there are plenty of people having a good time at the expense of that little pretence? Looking at the corpse of the god laid out flat, going off, swelling up, the way every body does? [pause] And by the way, Alexander — that thing you said was useful, the easy victories — it cost you most of the credit for what you actually achieved. Everything you did looked like it fell short of what a god should manage.

lines.speaker: Alexander
lines.text: That's not what people think of me. They rank me alongside Heracles and Dionysus. The rock of Aornos — neither of them took it. I took it on my own.

lines.speaker: Philip
lines.text: There — you hear yourself? That's the son of Ammon talking. Comparing himself to Heracles and Dionysus. [pause] Aren't you ashamed, Alexander? Aren't you ever going to unlearn the vanity, and know yourself, and grasp — at long last — that you're dead?
